opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Matthew 20:1–16 is a beautiful reading, but at first it can feel terribly unfair. If we were the workers who had been in the vineyard since early morning, working through the heat of the entire day, we probably would have been upset too. Imagine watching someone arrive at five o’clock, work for only a short time, and receive the same wage you received. Our immediate response would probably be, How is that fair?

But that uncomfortable feeling is exactly where Jesus begins teaching us something deeper. The landowner had not cheated the workers. He gave them exactly what he had promised. Their disappointment only began when they looked at what someone else received. What had been enough suddenly didn’t feel like enough because of comparison.

How often do we do the same thing? We work hard, sacrifice, remain faithful, struggle through difficult seasons, and then look around and wonder why someone else seems to receive the same—or perhaps even more—without enduring what we have endured. We think, But I worked harder. I gave more. I have been here longer.

Yet Jesus reminds us that God’s generosity toward another person does not take anything away from us.

There is also something incredibly beautiful here about salvation. Some people spend their entire lives walking with God. Others may wander for years and find Him much later. Some may even turn toward Him near the very end of their lives. And still, God receives them. His kingdom is not divided according to seniority. His mercy is not less generous because someone arrived late.

Perhaps those of us who have walked with God longer should not ask, Why does that person receive what I receive? Instead, we might recognize what a gift it has been to know Him for all those years. Being with God was never supposed to be the burden of the first workers. It was already the blessing.

And look at the landowner: he keeps returning to the marketplace. Morning, noon, afternoon, and even when the working day is nearly finished, he is still searching for people and inviting them into his vineyard.

That may be one of the most beautiful messages in this Gospel. God does not look at the person arriving late and say, You missed your opportunity. He continues to call them.

Come. There is still room for you.

What extraordinary generosity. And perhaps part of following Christ is learning to rejoice when that generosity reaches someone else instead of comparing their journey with our own. God’s goodness toward another person does not diminish His goodness toward us. There is enough mercy for all of us—even those who arrive at the final hour.
